title: Design an ATM Machine
statement:
Build a class `ATM` for a cash machine that holds banknotes worth $20, $50, $100, $200 and $500. Every count array below has 5 entries, one per note value in that order ($20 first, $500 last).

- `ATM()` creates a machine with no banknotes in it.
- `deposit(banknotesCount)` adds `banknotesCount[i]` notes of the `i`-th value to the machine.
- `withdraw(amount)` tries to pay out exactly `amount` dollars. It goes through the values from $500 down to $20 and, at each one, takes as many of the stored notes of that value as fit into what is still owed, then moves on; it never revisits an earlier choice, so a request can fail even if some other mix of notes would add up to `amount`. If nothing is owed at the end, those notes leave the machine and the method returns the 5 counts handed out. Otherwise it returns `[-1]` and the machine keeps all its notes.
constraints: At most 5000 calls in total are made to withdraw and deposit
withdraw and deposit are each called at least once
The sum of all banknotesCount[i] over all deposits is at most 10^9
notes:
## Intuition

The machine's rule is fixed: use the biggest notes first and never backtrack. So there is no search to do, only a faithful simulation. A brute-force version could hand out one note at a time, but amounts reach 10^9, so take all the notes of one value at once: `min(stored, floor(remaining / value))`. The only subtle part is that a failed request must not change anything, so plan the withdrawal first and commit it only when it succeeds.

## Approach

1. Keep `values` (the five note values) and `counts` (how many of each are stored).
2. `deposit` adds each entry of `banknotesCount` to `counts`.
3. `withdraw` walks the values from $500 down, setting `taken[i]` to the most notes of that value that fit into `remaining`, and subtracts their worth.
4. If `remaining` is not 0, return `[-1]` without touching `counts`.
5. Otherwise subtract `taken` from `counts` and return `taken`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `deposit([0,0,1,2,1])`: `counts = [0,0,1,2,1]`.
- `withdraw(600)`: one $500 leaves 100; $200 notes do not fit; one $100 leaves 0. Return `[0,0,1,0,1]`; `counts = [0,0,0,2,0]`.
- `deposit([0,1,0,1,1])`: `counts = [0,1,0,3,1]`.
- `withdraw(600)`: one $500 leaves 100; no $200 fits, no $100 stored, one $50 leaves 50, no $20 stored. 50 is still owed, so return `[-1]`.
- `withdraw(550)`: one $500, then one $50, leaving 0. Return `[0,1,0,0,1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per call: always five note values.
- Space: O(1): two arrays of five numbers.

## Pitfalls

- Do not change `counts` while planning; a rejected request must leave the machine untouched.
- Do not "fix" a failure by trying smaller notes instead: $60 from one $50 and three $20 notes is rejected, because the $50 is taken first.
- Counts and amounts reach 10^9, so take notes with division, not one at a time; in Java or C store counts as 64-bit integers.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `values` | the note values, $20 to $500 |
| `counts` | how many notes of each value the machine holds |
| `taken` | notes of each value planned for this withdrawal |
| `remaining` | dollars still owed during planning |
| `i` | index of the note value being handled |
